terms.meaning: Python's built-in testing library, which runs checks and reports which ones failed.
A temporary folder created for a test and deleted when the test ends.
A fake explanation written by a test in place of a real model's answer.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Test setup and sample code
sections.what: Loads the tool and stores two sample source files, one in Python and one in JavaScript. The other tests write these samples into temporary folders.
sections.why: Gives every test the same known input so results can be compared.
sections.watch_out: Tests check exact names and line numbers in these samples, so changing them will break expected results.

sections.name: first
sections.title: Sample function used in tests
sections.what: A tiny Python function in the sample that returns its first item.
sections.why: Gives the section-splitting test a named function to look for.

sections.name: Box
sections.title: Sample class used in tests
sections.what: A tiny Python class in the sample with one method that returns a stored value.
sections.why: Lets the tests confirm that classes are split into their own sections.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Sample program start point
sections.what: The run-if-main block at the end of the Python sample, which prints the result of the sample function.
sections.why: Lets the tests confirm that a file's entry point is recognised as its own section.

sections.name: run
sections.title: Helper that runs a tool command
sections.what: Runs one clarity command in the same process, captures what it prints, and returns its exit code and printed text.
sections.why: Lets each test check both the result and the message a user would see.
sections.watch_out: Commands run in the same process, so settings such as the working folder carry between calls.

sections.name: answer_for
sections.title: Writes fake explanations for every section
sections.what: Builds an answer in the same shape a real explainer would produce, with a short sentence per section and placeholder file fields.
sections.why: The tests make no model calls, so this stands in for the explaining step.
sections.watch_out: The fake answers are always marked needs-work, so passing tests do not show that real explanations are good.

sections.name: SectionSplitting
sections.title: Checks how code is cut into sections
sections.what: Confirms that sections in Python, JavaScript and SQL cover every line with no gaps or overlaps, that small helper functions keep their names, and that a very long function is split.
sections.why: Each section gets its own note, so a gap or overlap would lose or duplicate notes.
sections.watch_out: The size check uses the tool's section size limit, so changing that limit changes what counts as too long.

sections.name: EndToEnd (part 1)
sections.title: Full cycle test on a throwaway project
sections.what: Creates a sample project with two source files and a node_modules folder, runs sync, fills every note with fake answers, runs strict checks, and builds the page. It then confirms the page holds the sample summary and no empty data slot.
sections.why: Shows the whole chain of commands works from start to finish.
sections.watch_out: The explain helper stops after ten rounds, so a note that never finishes appears as a failed test rather than a hang.

sections.name: EndToEnd: test_changed_code_loses_only_its_own_notes_and_undo_restores_them
sections.title: Checks that edits only redo changed notes
sections.what: Changes one function and confirms that only that function needs a new note and the file summary is marked stale. It then restores the original text and confirms that every note is complete again.
sections.why: Prevents a small code change from forcing a rewrite of every note.
sections.watch_out: The undo is a plain rewrite of the original text, so the test depends on the content matching exactly.

sections.name: Publishing
sections.title: Publish safety and republish tests
sections.what: Builds a temporary fake project and portfolio folder, then checks three things about the publish command. A full publish is refused when the code contains a secret-looking token. A notes-only publish succeeds without putting any code on the page. Publishing the same project twice leaves only one entry in the manifest, the index file that lists published projects.
sections.why: Likely reason: the publish tool must not leak secrets, so these checks guard that rule and stop the listing from filling with duplicates.
sections.watch_out: The setup changes the GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES environment setting, and the teardown only restores the working folder, so later tests in the same run inherit that setting.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Runs the tests when executed directly
sections.what: When this file is run on its own, it runs every test in the file and prints each test name with its result.
sections.why: Likely reason: this is the usual way to make a Python test file runnable from the command line.

summary: Self-test that builds a throwaway sample project and checks that each clarity command splits, explains, checks, builds and publishes correctly.
purpose: Confirms the clarity tool works on this machine without touching the real repository or calling any model.
why: The file header says its purpose is to show the tool works on this machine, so the checks run on a known sample before anyone trusts real results.
how: Writes sample Python and JavaScript files into a temporary folder, runs each clarity command against them, fills in fake explanations with the answer helper, checks the saved notes and generated page, then removes the temporary folder.
inputs: Sample source text stored in this file, and the clarity module in the folder above the tests.
outputs: A list of passed and failed tests printed by unittest.
risks: The tests change the current working folder and set the GIT_CEILING_DIRECTORIES environment setting. They restore the folder but do not restore that setting. A failure in the temporary setup can hide real problems.
debug: Run the file with python3 and read the first failing test name and its message. If git-related tests fail, confirm the temporary folder is outside any git repository. The header gives a run path under .claude, but this file sits under tools/clarity, so use the path that exists.
